newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil rate policy seen unaffected by Fed move.
newsitem.headline: Brazil rate policy seen unaffected by Fed move.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Board's 25 basis point rise in short-term U.S. interest rates should not affect Brazil's current monetary policy, which could withstand another 50 basis point increase over the year, economists said.

Brazil's current policy of gradually cutting interest rates each month would continue until rates hit their natural floor, which will be determined more by domestic than international factors, analysts added.
"Up to this moment Brazil has plenty of external financing," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at BMC bank in Brazil.
"Even if we suppose that this is just the first of three 25 basis point hikes over the year, then we don't believe the Brazilian Central Bank will change its monetary policy," Allain said.

Economists said Brazil's country risk had improved measurably among international investors over the past year, noting it would take more than a gradual 75 basis point rise in short-term U.S. rates to cause foreign capital to flow out of Brazil.
Still, Brazil's steady, four basis point decline in monthly rates since October was not seen lasting forever.

"Interest rates are getting close to the floor. But the Central Bank will slow rate cuts or stop them for domestic reasons, not because they think the Fed will hike rates by 75 basis points over the year," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist at J.P. Morgan in Brazil.

J.P. Morgan, which believes Tuesday's Fed move was the first of three 25 basis point rises this year, forecasts that Brazil's Central Bank will continue cutting monthly interest rates until they reach 1.54 percent from about 1.63 percent now.
A Reuter survey of eight Brazilian banks and brokerages forecasts the Central Bank will stop cutting Brazilian rates when they reach 1.45 percent.

Brazil set interest rates at a high of about 4.0 percent a month in April 1995 to slow the economy and attract foreign dollars in the wake of the Mexican peso crisis. The Central Bank began slashing interest rates in late 1995.
Real interest rates in Brazil fell from about 30 percent in 1995 to 17 percent in 1996 and are expected to fall to about 10 percent this year.
